title: Jorgensen Gallery: “Flesh and Fable” Exhibition
organizer: Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts (University of Connecticut)
description: Afarin Rahmanifar, M.F.A., is an Iranian American mixed-media artist, curator, educator, and Associate Professor of Painting and Drawing at Eastern Connecticut State University, where she has taught since 2013. Born in Iran and displaced after the 1979 Revolution, her work is shaped by themes of memory, exile, identity, and transformation. Using fragmented anatomical forms, Persian visual traditions, and the women of the Shahnameh, she examines how memory and cultural inheritance shape identity and belonging. Through painting, drawing, collage, textile, and mixed media, she layers and reconstructs the female body as an act of remembrance and reclamation— honoring women whose stories have been overlooked or silenced.

title: Math Club: Introduction to the Hyperbolic Plane, by Ben Schussler (UConn)
description: Written in the fourth century BC and widely used up until the 19th century, Euclid’s Elements is an ancient mathematical textbook which derives many fundamental facts about geometry from just five basic assumptions. For almost 2,000 years, mathematicians sought to prove that the fifth of those axioms, called the parallel postulate, was actually a consequence of the other four. This task was only shown to be impossible in the mid-1800s with the creation of the hyperbolic plane. Hyperbolic geometry, and the resulting field of non-Euclidean geometry, has had far-reaching implications for mathematics, philosophy, and physics, and served as inspiration for artists and authors like M.C. Escher and H.P. Lovecraft. This talk will discuss the history and construction of the hyperbolic plane, and explore some of its unintuitive features with virtual and physical interactive models.

description: CCAM Seminar Series Speaker: Dr. Timothy Duerr Ph.D., Assistant Professor, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, UConn Health Title: “Cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating proximodistal positional identity during axolotl limb regeneration” Abstract: Axolotl salamanders can regenerate their limbs following amputation anywhere along the proximodistal (PD) axis. During this process, resident connective tissue cells, including dermal fibroblasts and periskeletal cells, dedifferentiate and accumulate at the limb stump to form a blastema. Blastema cells retain their genetically encoded PD positional identity, enabling them to redifferentiate and regenerate the appropriate PD limb structures. Retinoic acid (RA) signaling is essential for establishing PD positional identity, as elevated levels of RA instruct blastema cells to adopt a proximal limb identity. We found that RA concentration along the PD axis is regulated by Cyp26b1 expression, which degrades excess RA to generate distal identity during limb regeneration. These differences in RA concentration lead to differential expression of homeobox genes that provide blastema cells with the correct PD positional identity. One such gene identified was Shox, which we show is required for activation of the PTHrP/IHH feedback loop in regenerating chondrocytes of proximally amputated limbs. Once blastema cells genetically adopt positional identity via RA, they express PD-specific cell surface proteins that modify cellular adhesivity. This enables self-sorting with cells of similar positional identities. We have identified several cell surface proteins, including LPHN2, TENM4, and FLRT3 that follow the same spatiotemporal expression patterns as 5’ Hox genes and are both RA responsive and differentially expressed between proximally and distally amputated limbs. description: Host: Jill Desimini Location: YNG 132 Join Remotely: s.uconn.edu/psla_seminars Other Ways of Building In contrast to modern and colonial architectures, Anishinaabe building practices and the worldviews they embody represent a fundamentally different approach to design. The Traditional Ecological Knowledge systems indigenous to the Great Lakes challenge the common understanding of objects and buildings as fixed or stable, instead conceptualizing them as always in flux, and therefore impermanent. title: Jorgensen Gallery: “Flesh and Fable” Exhibition
organizer: Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts (University of Connecticut)
description: Afarin Rahmanifar, M.F.A., is an Iranian American mixed-media artist, curator, educator, and Associate Professor of Painting and Drawing at Eastern Connecticut State University, where she has taught since 2013. Born in Iran and displaced after the 1979 Revolution, her work is shaped by themes of memory, exile, identity, and transformation. Using fragmented anatomical forms, Persian visual traditions, and the women of the Shahnameh, she examines how memory and cultural inheritance shape identity and belonging. Through painting, drawing, collage, textile, and mixed media, she layers and reconstructs the female body as an act of remembrance and reclamation— honoring women whose stories have been overlooked or silenced.

title: Jorgensen Gallery: “Flesh and Fable” Exhibition
organizer: Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts (University of Connecticut)
description: Afarin Rahmanifar, M.F.A., is an Iranian American mixed-media artist, curator, educator, and Associate Professor of Painting and Drawing at Eastern Connecticut State University, where she has taught since 2013. Born in Iran and displaced after the 1979 Revolution, her work is shaped by themes of memory, exile, identity, and transformation. Using fragmented anatomical forms, Persian visual traditions, and the women of the Shahnameh, she examines how memory and cultural inheritance shape identity and belonging. Through painting, drawing, collage, textile, and mixed media, she layers and reconstructs the female body as an act of remembrance and reclamation— honoring women whose stories have been overlooked or silenced.

title: Nostalgia for the Crusades in Late Medieval England
organizer: Center for Learning in Retirement (University of Connecticut)
description: The crusade era is traditionally said to begin with the fall of Jerusalem to Western European armies in 1099 and to end with the fall of Acre, the last Christian fortress, in 1291, to Muslim Mamluk forces. The idea of a new crusade to recapture Jerusalem and the surrounding “Holy Land,” however, lived on in the European imagination. This class will focus on crusade fantasies in late 14th century English literature. There is the ultraviolent (Richard Coeur de Lion) as well as the ironic (Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales). We will focus on an intriguing aspect of this literature, a desire to emulate the Mongol Empire, imagined as an ascendant Eastern power in contrast to a decadent West. We will also touch on some current crusade fantasies and their role in Islamophobia and “holy war.” Ruth Nisse, Professor, Department of English, Center for Jewish Studies, Wesleyan University CLIR is a fee-based program. Please visit clir.uconn.edu for more information.

title: Mathematics Colloquium by Jonathan Weitsman (Northeastern)
description: Title: What is Symplectic Geometry? Speaker: Jonathan Weitsman (Northeastern University) Abstract: Symplectic Geometry, which has its origins in Classical Mechanics, has become an important area of Differential Geometry. Nevertheless the geometric picture of what a symplectic manifold “looks like” has not been so clear. Alan Weinstein provided insight into this question by studying morphisms of symplectic manifolds, giving rise to a Symplectic “Category”. The scare quotes are due to the fact that transversality troubles mean composition is not quite well-defined. In this talk we plan to review the origins of Symplectic Geometry, explain Weinstein’s proposal, and show how to construct a true category morally dual to Weinstein’s “category”. Along the way we will encounter superalgebras and an application to Geometric Quantization. (Arxiv reference 2608.09681)

description: CCAM Seminar Series Speaker: Dr. Timothy Duerr Ph.D., Assistant Professor, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, UConn Health Title: “Cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating proximodistal positional identity during axolotl limb regeneration” Abstract: Axolotl salamanders can regenerate their limbs following amputation anywhere along the proximodistal (PD) axis. During this process, resident connective tissue cells, including dermal fibroblasts and periskeletal cells, dedifferentiate and accumulate at the limb stump to form a blastema. Blastema cells retain their genetically encoded PD positional identity, enabling them to redifferentiate and regenerate the appropriate PD limb structures. Retinoic acid (RA) signaling is essential for establishing PD positional identity, as elevated levels of RA instruct blastema cells to adopt a proximal limb identity. We found that RA concentration along the PD axis is regulated by Cyp26b1 expression, which degrades excess RA to generate distal identity during limb regeneration. These differences in RA concentration lead to differential expression of homeobox genes that provide blastema cells with the correct PD positional identity. One such gene identified was Shox, which we show is required for activation of the PTHrP/IHH feedback loop in regenerating chondrocytes of proximally amputated limbs. Once blastema cells genetically adopt positional identity via RA, they express PD-specific cell surface proteins that modify cellular adhesivity. This enables self-sorting with cells of similar positional identities. We have identified several cell surface proteins, including LPHN2, TENM4, and FLRT3 that follow the same spatiotemporal expression patterns as 5’ Hox genes and are both RA responsive and differentially expressed between proximally and distally amputated limbs. title: Propagating Native Plants to Benefit Endangered Animal Species
organizer: Center for Learning in Retirement (University of Connecticut)
description: Native plants are often key players in endangered animal life cycles. For this talk the speaker will explore different plant propagation techniques and projects he has studied for several years. Specifically the speaker will discuss growing wild indigo and sundial lupine as larval host plants for the state threatened frosted elfin butterfly. A second project covered in this talk involved the division of seaside goldenrod to benefit common tern nesting habitat on Great Gull Island in Long Island Sound. Additionally the speaker will cover propagation of several watch list or endangered milkweeds, which are important for monarch butterflies. Bryan Connolly, Associate Professor of Biology, ECSU CLIR is a fee-based program. Please visit clir.uconn.edu for more information.

organizer: Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts (University of Connecticut)
description: Afarin Rahmanifar, M.F.A., is an Iranian American mixed-media artist, curator, educator, and Associate Professor of Painting and Drawing at Eastern Connecticut State University, where she has taught since 2013. Born in Iran and displaced after the 1979 Revolution, her work is shaped by themes of memory, exile, identity, and transformation. Using fragmented anatomical forms, Persian visual traditions, and the women of the Shahnameh, she examines how memory and cultural inheritance shape identity and belonging. Through painting, drawing, collage, textile, and mixed media, she layers and reconstructs the female body as an act of remembrance and reclamation— honoring women whose stories have been overlooked or silenced.

title: Mathematics colloquium by Frank Quan (UIUC)
description: Title: Automating the Insurance Analytics Pipeline: Rigorous Data Preparation, AutoML, and Domain-Adapted Language Models. Speaker: Frank Quan (UIUC) Abstract: Data science is increasingly adopted in actuarial research and insurance practice, yet its reliability depends on every stage of the workflow, from data preparation to model building to operational decisions, in a regulated, data-sensitive industry. This talk follows that pipeline through three connected contributions. We begin with data preparation, showing that conventional practices like random train-test partitioning produce unstable results on highly imbalanced insurance loss data. We propose a statistically principled alternative: support points for representative splitting, Chatterjee’s correlation coefficient for non-parametric feature screening, and integrated missing-data handling. Evaluations on simulated and benchmark datasets demonstrate improved robustness and interpretability at lower computational cost. We then embed these methods in InsurAutoML, an insurance-tailored automated machine learning framework whose data balancing, ensemble pipelines, and customized loss functions let non-expert users deploy robust models with a few lines of code. Finally, moving from prediction to decision support, we use millions of historical warranty claims to fine-tune locally deployed large language models via Low-Rank Adaptation, generating structured corrective-action recommendations from unstructured claim narratives. Domain-adaptive fine-tuning substantially outperforms general-purpose LLMs, with about 98% of cases closely matching ground truth. Together, these results point toward trustworthy, governable automation across the insurance analytics pipeline.

description: Afarin Rahmanifar, M.F.A., is an Iranian American mixed-media artist, curator, educator, and Associate Professor of Painting and Drawing at Eastern Connecticut State University, where she has taught since 2013. Born in Iran and displaced after the 1979 Revolution, her work is shaped by themes of memory, exile, identity, and transformation. Using fragmented anatomical forms, Persian visual traditions, and the women of the Shahnameh, she examines how memory and cultural inheritance shape identity and belonging. Through painting, drawing, collage, textile, and mixed media, she layers and reconstructs the female body as an act of remembrance and reclamation— honoring women whose stories have been overlooked or silenced.
